articles.text: Three key presentations are scheduled for the May 28 school board meeting, including recognitions for retiring staff and this year’s four school board members. The board will also hold a first reading of proposed changes to next year’s elementary English Language Arts curriculum, a process that has been years in the making. Following the presentation, the ELA Adoption Committee will formally recommend replacing the current Lucy Calkins-authored curriculum with Fishtank Learning at Beach, Havens, and Wildwood. Although the resolution directs the district to fly the Pride flag only during June, since October 2024 the current practice has been to display it year-round. articles.text: On Friday, May 23, fourthgrade students from Ben Spencer and Alicia Martinez’s classes at Beach School participated in a community service field trip, collecting 120 pounds of trash. In small groups led by parent volunteers, students fanned out across neighborhoods in Piedmont and Oakland, gathering 4,690 individual pieces of litter in just two hours. Back on campus, students cataloged every item before weighing the total haul. Among the debris were paper plates, cigarette butts, food wrappers and orange peels—evidence that even everyday waste can end up in unexpected and unwanted places. Wearing gloves, tongs and safety goggles, students explored local parks and streets, including the Rose Garden, Piedmont Avenue, Grand Avenue, Pleasant Valley and Dracena Park. articles.text: Editor: From the music of Grease to Gustav Holst’s Jupiter, the Piedmont High School and Piedmont Middle School bands and orchestras performed last week, an inspiring musical celebration to cap the school year. But our district’s sterling music program is now being threatened. Recently, the school board approved a program to end instrumental music education for fourth graders, an unnecessarily rushed move that is short-sighted and will limit the musical potential of our students. Learning an instrument takes time, and it requires repeated hands-on practice to become proficient enough to play more than “Hot Cross Buns.” Delaying instrumental music education means that students will have less of an opportunity to master an instrument. It will have a major impact on middle and high school band and orchestra. And students will lose out on the cognitive benefits that come from learning an instrument. Elementary and middle school students have recently complained about a frustrating music experience. Instead of fixing this problem – such as hiring a full-time music teacher or incorporating more classroom support – Piedmont threw the baby out with the bathwater. Our fourth graders will now get 60 minutes a week of “theater arts.” The school board heralded this as an exciting change. While we love what theater offers for kids, it should not come at the expense of music. Our kids already have ready access to theater, including in the classroom. But there are few opportunities for students to try a variety of instruments and perform in groups. Now they won’t have that chance until 5th grade. Our neighboring school districts – including Berkeley, Orinda, Lafayette, and Moraga – introduce instruments in the fourth grade. With regression such as this, we will continue to lose students to private schools. Our district is not being innovative. It is taking a step back in the musical education it offers to our students. articles.text: Piedmont Unified School District awarded Cory Smegal the 2025 Arthur Hecht Award as the school volunteer of the year. She was presented with the award during the May 14 school board meeting. Smegal served two terms on the school board from 2016-2024. During her eight year tenure on the school board Smegal bridged the gap from pre- to post-pandemic education in Piedmont. Education and volunteering is a family tradition. Cory’s mother in-law, Sue Smegal, won the award in 2020 and was a member of the school board. “Thanks to Sue, for not only convincing Tom [husband] and me to move to Piedmont but she was also so inspiring with her years of service,” said Cory. “Thanks for being such a strong example of leadership and community involvement and community support.” Cor y’s legacy includes reopening the schools after the pandemic and pushing for the building of the STEAM building and Alan Harvey Theater. Before holding public office she volunteered tirelessly by raising money for the Giving Campaign and the middle school via March Mingle. “Cory is optimistic and enthusiastic. She believes in the best of people and thinks creatively to solve problems. She is ridiculously smart and has forgotten more about the district than others could aspire to know,” said Vice President Ruchi Medhekar. Piedmont Mayor, Betsy Smegal Andersen is Cory’s sister-inlaw. “When you ran for school board you knew it was going to be a lot of work but you didn’t know Covid was coming. But the second time you ran, you did know Covid was coming,” said Andersen. term in 2020, Smegal provided continuity in leadership and a steady hand when the schools were closed due to Covid. Smegal sought reelection to the board despite the microscope upon school board members and education decision makers across the globe. “Some of our meetings during Covid had several hundred people. There’s nothing like an experience of breaking down in tears and sobbing in front of hundreds of people, so I’m trying not to cry tonight,” said Cory. Smegal’s fingerprints on the district are easy to see. She served on the board while hiring Interim-Superintendent Donald Evans, and current Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. The award is named for Art Hecht, a former school Board member and a tireless community volunteer in Piedmont and Oakland schools. He served on Piedmont’s Board of Education from 1970 to 1982. He was very active with the founding of the Piedmont Continuation High School (now called Millennium High School). articles.text: Construction, road work block both sides of Piedmont’s busiest street Signage now marks detours for temporary sidewalk closures on Grand Avenue, between Oakland and Linda Avenues. The closure prevents pedestrian traffic on both sides of the street due to an apparent breakdown of communication between a housing construction project and the ongoing Grand Avenue Repavement Project. Piedmont resident and Greenbank Neighborhood Watch Coordinator Mark Herrick first noticed the safety issue presented by the sidewalk closures three weeks ago. “It caught me off-guard that they weren’t aware of this problem,” he said. After almost three weeks of correspondence with the City, Herrick sent in a video after repeatedly being told that the sidewalk should still be accessible from the other side. The City has since updated the signage to include detours on both sides of the street. “It sure took a lot of effort and frankly a lot of broken glass, because I had to jump up and down and send some hard emails to get them to listen to me,” said Herrick about the City’s less-than-satisfactory response. Herrick reported difficulty getting members of City Council involved, with one excepNew detour signage directs pedestrians away from construction areas. tion. While Herrick struggled to get the City to understand and recognize the safety issue, Councilmember Lorrell Plimier seemed to show genuine concern. “She was sensitive to the issues, she responded to me directly, she came down to my house… and she saw the problems and she saw that there was really poor signage that was not clear. And as a result of her coming, things got better,” said Herrick. With construction of new pedestrian bulb-outs on Grand Avenue underway, officials remind community members to follow instructions on safety signage and use marked detours. The pedestrian crossings will remain closed at the intersections of Grand Avenue with Linda and Greenbank Avenues while electrical infrastructure is being installed to support flashing safety beacons. Closures will continue until bulb-out construction is complete, expected in June. The work is part of a $1.5 million roadway improvement and pedestrian safety project on Grand Ave., funded in part by a $500,000 grant from the Alameda County Transportation Commission. The work includes bulb-outs and flashing beacons at the Linda and Greenbank intersections, as well as bicycle safety enhancements and ADA curb ramps at all street crossings. Once bulb-outs at Linda and Greenback Avenues are complete, construction will begin at the intersection of Grand and Fairview. There, the City will install permanent bulb-out islands and a bioswale – a landscaped channel that improves drainage and supports soil filtering of storm water. The final phase of the project, scheduled for August, will re-pave Grand Avenue from Fairview to Greenbank. Roadside construction has caused changes to pedestrian pathways along Grand Avenue.

articles.text: 2-week trip to raise awareness of autism A group of students from Piedmont High School, HeadRoyce School, and other high schools will travel to Ethiopia this June for a two-week service and advocacy trip focused on autism awareness and education. The initiative is being led by Nathan Bekele, a junior at Piedmont High School, as a part of his membership in the Piedmont Community Service Crew and in partnership with the Melu’e Foundation. Through the Ethiopian Ministry of Health, Bekele was able to establish the connection and secure a partnership with the foundation that supports children with autism and their families. The goal of the trip is to raise awareness of the stigma of autism in Ethiopia where affected children are often isolated from their communities. The local students will visit schools and community centers in Addis Ababa to host educational workshops, volunteer at the Melu’e Foundation’s multidisciplinary treatment center – one of only two autism centers in the entire country – and deliver equipment and the supplies needed by the center for children and families. Joaquin Fierro, a freshman at Piedmont High School, says, “I’m looking forward to making a meaningful impact on those in need, while also being able to explore a new and exciting culture. “I really want to help kids that need it the most. I am also excited to share this experience with my friends,” said Bekele. The trip will begin on June 10 and conclude on June 29. The service trip was made possible in part by Bekele’s “Taste of Ethiopia with Jazz” fundraiser dinner hosted at Lemat Restaurant in Berkeley, which raised over $35,000 to support the initiative. Tax deductible donations may be made to: https://givebutter. com/NathanforAutism The students look forward to reporting their experiences after they return from the trip. articles.text: Volunteers for Nature Program Manager, California Academy of Sciences Get involved: rediscover local nature through volunteering Volunteering is more than lending a hand—it’s a meaningful way to connect with your community, spend time outdoors, and make a tangible difference close to home. Whether you’re newly retired, raising a family, or simply looking to give back, nature-based volunteer opportunities offer a chance to support the environment while boosting your own well-being. At the California Academy of Sciences, we offer a variety of local volunteer programs—both inside the museum and out in the community. One of our recent pilots, Volunteers for Nature, engaged college students and early-career professionals in regeneration projects across the Bay Area. In our latest initiative with the Presidio Trust, volunteers helped restore San Francisco’s sand dunes by supporting the silvery blue butterfly, a species that symbolizes the extinct Xerces blue, last seen in the Presidio in the 1940s. Efforts like these help revive local ecosystems—and they’re open to everyone. which is essential to supporting pollinators. Search for local conservation organizations to see what’s happening near you. If plants aren’t your thing, consider joining Snapshot Cal Coast, a statewide effort to document coastal biodiversity—either solo or at a local bioblitz. Or, join Wild Oyster Project in Alameda for monthly volunteer days working to restore native oysters to the Bay. Why volunteer? Beyond the measurable impact on ecosystems, research shows that volunteering can improve mental health, enhance physical wellness, and develop skills like empathy and patience. For those early in their careers, it can even boost employment prospects. According to the Corporation for National and Community Service, volunteers are 27% more likely to find a job. Volunteering invites us to connect—with nature, with others, and with ourselves. As John Muir once said, “Go out to go in.” So let’s get to work. You don’t need to travel far to make a difference. Whether it’s a local park, shoreline cleanup, or community garden, your efforts matter. If we don’t know our local nature, how can we protect it? Let’s rediscover it—together. Ready to get started? June is Pollinator Month, the perfect time to jump into volunteering. Many opportunities focus on native plant restoration, If you are interested in more information about CAL Academy, check out calacademy.org or call at (415) 379-8000 Volunteers for Nature participants help install native plant species in the Presidio.
articles.title: Step into nature: how volunteering can help you and the planet thrive

articles.text: The distant hum of the freeway and the occasional train horn could faintly be heard all the way to Palm Drive. Birds chirped in the trees to greet the early sun, filling the quiet morning. Palm trees towered over the still-sleeping houses. A blue-and-gold lawn sign that read, “Congratulations Class of ’25,” stood in front of the house with a crawling bougainvillea still wet with dew from the night before. Somewhere inside that house, a faucet turned on, an alarm rang, and a dog barked. The sun rose higher in the sky. At the end of the street, the red stop sign saw more and more cars as the world began to wake. A squirrel perched on a tree branch watched dogs and their owners emerge from their homes for morning walks. It remained unseen—its sworn enemies oblivious as they passed below. It chittered once and leapt to another tree. In front of the house with the blue-and-gold sign, a car engine sputtered to life—a gray Volkswagen, to be exact. It made its way past the red stop sign, up Oakland Avenue, across Highland, through Moraga Canyon, and onto Highway 13. From there, it merged onto Highway 24 and passed through the Caldecott Tunnel into Orinda. The greenand-yellow hills rolled above the morning commuters. The Volkswagen took Exit 11, turned right, went down the hill past the “Bentley Upper School” sign, and pulled through the campus gates. The student lot wasn’t full yet—classes wouldn’t start for another 15 minutes. The metallic roofs of the gym and English buildings began to glow as the sun’s rays danced across them. More cars arrived, more students walked up the steps to campus. The clock ticked closer to 8:30. When it finally struck 8:30, teachers began their morning lessons—everything from the principles of statistics to the fall of the Roman Empire. The campus was quiet, or as quiet as it could be with a freeway nearby. Aside from that, only the occasional buzz of a leaf blower or the sound of a tardy slip printing in the front office broke the silence. From the commons came the smell of lunch and the chatter of students enjoying a free period away from the chilly morning air. The day unfolded. Classes began and ended, homework turned in and new assignments handed out. Above the school, vultures circled in the sky, riding the wind currents, looking down at the people below. Then the wind shifted, and the vultures drifted off. Lunch came. Seniors with off-campus privileges left with friends. Students lay on the field in the warm sun. The gym echoed with shouts and friendly competition. Tables in the quad filled with conversation and food. The commons, as always, held its familiar lunch line. It was a break from academics, and students made the most of it. The seniors talked about life after high school. Graduation felt near. The final classes of the day began. Inside air-conditioned classrooms, teachers handed out more readings, more worksheets, more instructions. At the front office, small talk spilled through open doors. Another off-campus pass was dated and signed. Pleasantries exchanged, a student began the walk back to the parking lot. The gray Volkswagen’s lights flashed as it unlocked. The engine came to life once more, and the car exited through campus and headed back toward the hilltop gate. Its left blinker came on, the accelerator pressed, and the journey home began—through the hills, through the tunnel, back onto Highway 13, down Moraga Canyon, across Highland, down Oakland, and finally to the house with the blue-and-gold sign and the blooming red bougainvillea. The day began to wind down. The stop sign welcomed home the same cars it had seen in the morning. The squirrel had vanished into the trees. The sun dipped lower. Another day had wound down. In the house with the blue-and-gold sign, two sisters were about to graduate: one ready to toss her high school cap, the other her college one. A plane ride to a university in Scotland waited for one. A new job to start for the other. Things were ending, yes—but just as many things were beginning. When both graduates finally walk across their separate stages and receive their diplomas, their parents’ applause will rise above all the rest—as it always has, and always will. It’s frightening when the routines and places we’ve grown used to fall away, but that only means there are new places to discover, and new routines to create. To the graduating class of 2025: congratulations. We finally made it. As we head to different corners of the world, remember the places and patterns you once called home—for they’ll always be there to welcome you back. Piedmont resident Larissa Edel is a graduating senior at Bentley School, an intern with the Post and a contributing writer for six years.
articles.title: As the school year winds down

Step into nature: how volunteering can help you and the planet thrive By Julia Weber Volunteers for Nature Program Manager, California Academy of Sciences Get involved: rediscover local nature through volunteering Volunteering is more than lending a hand—it’s a meaningful way to connect with your community, spend time outdoors, and make a tangible difference close to home. Whether you’re newly retired, raising a family, or simply looking to give back, nature-based volunteer opportunities offer a chance to support the environment while boosting your own well-being. At the California Academy of Sciences, we offer a variety of local volunteer programs—both inside the museum and out in the community. One of our recent pilots, Volunteers for Nature, engaged college students and early-career professionals in regeneration projects across the Bay Area. In our latest initiative with the Presidio Trust, volunteers helped restore San Francisco’s sand dunes by supporting the silvery blue butterfly, a species that symbolizes the extinct Xerces blue, last seen in the Presidio in the 1940s. Efforts like these help revive local ecosystems—and they’re open to everyone. which is essential to supporting pollinators. Search for local conservation organizations to see what’s happening near you. If plants aren’t your thing, consider joining Snapshot Cal Coast, a statewide effort to document coastal biodiversity—either solo or at a local bioblitz. Or, join Wild Oyster Project in Alameda for monthly volunteer days working to restore native oysters to the Bay. Why volunteer? Beyond the measurable impact on ecosystems, research shows that volunteering can improve mental health, enhance physical wellness, and develop skills like empathy and patience. For those early in their careers, it can even boost employment prospects. According to the Corporation for National and Community Service, volunteers are 27% more likely to find a job. Volunteering invites us to connect—with nature, with others, and with ourselves. As John Muir once said, “Go out to go in.” So let’s get to work. You don’t need to travel far to make a difference. Whether it’s a local park, shoreline cleanup, or community garden, your efforts matter. If we don’t know our local nature, how can we protect it? Let’s rediscover it—together. Ready to get started? June is Pollinator Month, the perfect time to jump into volunteering. articles.text: Swain only athlete to qualify for State Championship Piedmont High’s track and field team took to Dublin High School on Friday and Saturday, May 23-24 for the 2025 North Coast Section Meet of Champions. The Highlanders brought a total of 19 athletes to compete across 18 different events, while athletes with top three finishes qualify for the prestigious CIF State Championship in Clovis. Sophomore Sebastien Swain was Piedmont’s only athlete to qualify for the State meet after finishing 2nd in the 800 meters with a time of 1:54.67. He was a half second behind the winning runner, Caeden Gardner, a senior from Tamalpais. Swain was in a field of 12 runners. The previous day he was fifth of 22 half milers in the prelims in 1:57.08. “Seb put together back to back weeks with beautifully executed races, said coach Pouyan Assadi. “He runs the event like a veteran. He’ll have his work cut out for him next week, but none of us ever doubted what he’s capable of,” RT Reaching the State Championship puts a bow on another strong athletic campaign. In the fall Swain also reached the CIF State Cross Country Championship in November, making the upcoming State run the third of his two-year high school career thus far. Swain also ran the third leg of the 4x400 relay team alongside Maddox Ma, Eric Venner, and Sam Shelby. The foursome finished sixth of 22 teams in the prelims with a time of 3:27.66, then advanced to the finals to finish ninth in 3:30.57. Here’s a rundown of all results from the NCS Meet of Champions. In her first year on the varsity team, Nia Kim made the NCS Meet of Champions finals in the 100 meter hurdles. Photos by Becky Spies Sebastien Swain (#5) qualified for the CIF State Championship by finishing second in the 800 meters at the North Coast Section Meet of Champions. Meet Recap Nia Kim reached the finals of the 100 meter hurdles, finishing sixth of eight with a time of 15.19 seconds. To reach the finals, Kim was fifth of 23 in the prelims in 15.30. Kim has been a standout story on this year’s track and field team. She joined the team as a senior after being a gymnast in her earlier years in high school. Initially joining track with the intention of being a sprinter, coach Assadi noticed she had a quick understanding of hurdling after seeing her in practice. ‘ “This season was the first step in what will certainly be a wonderful track and field career for Nia. We’re excited that UC Santa Cruz is going to take a shot on her. I said to her on Saturday that all of this is a stepping stone for the next level,” Assadi said. Kim also competed on two relay teams. She was the first leg in the 4x100 with Ella Yasar, Kyla Williams, and Claire Aubrecht, which finished the prelims 17th of 24 in 50.18. articles.text: Season ends in North Coast Section Quarterfinals Piedmont High’s baseball season came to an end on Friday, May 23, falling as the No. 2 seed to No. 10 Northgate 5-0 at Humphries Diamond in the quarterfinals of the Division 3 North Coast Section playoffs. The game was similar to PHS’ WACC Semifinals loss to Encinal on May 12, where a pitcher threw lightsout baseball. This time, NAME pitched 6.1 innings for the Broncos, recording 10 strikeouts and two hits allowed. “We’ve faced some really good left-handed pitchers this year. That kid threw hard and he tossed like 107 pitches, we couldn’t get him out of the game. Give him credit, we just couldn’t get consecutive at bats,” coach Eric Olson said. PHS gave up individual runs in the top of the first, third, and fifth innings before allowing two in the seventh. The Highlanders won six games in come-from-behind fashion this season, including their recent 7-6 win over No. 15 Archie Williams in the first round, but they couldn’t reactivate the comeback on Friday. “It was the strength of our team because we always had hope, character, and heart. But she finally bucked us off, we got down and couldn’t claw back. That’s a well-coached quality team. But I’m super proud of our guys. To be bumped up to Division 3 and play bigger schools when we’ve always been D4, it’s a feather in the cap of our guys,” Olson said. “Basically all four of my years, we’ve been a team that crept up on guys, but today we couldn’t do it. It was still a strong year, I don’t think we’ve ever played in Division 3 before. Hopefully, we left an impact on younger freshmen to keep this going,” added senior outfielder Markos Lagios. Piedmont had a chance to make some damage when Will Parker cracked a triple off the right-center field fence with no outs in the fourth inning, but the Highlanders went down with three straight strikeouts. “He was jamming me, so I stepped off the plate. He was tough though, I think our approach was a little bit off today, but that’s baseball. We had a few good comebacks, but going down 5-0 makes things tough and it’s easier to put up a run here and there. If I’m brought in, it becomes 2-1 and you never know how that changes a game. We just didn’t get those runs today,” Parker said. Will Parker celebrates after sliding into third base with at triple. Markos Lagios wraps up his illustrious athletic career at Piedmont High. Staff Photos Piedmont’s season came to an end on May 23, losing to Northgate in the D3 NCS Quarterfinals. “We always work to get a guy [on base] and get him in. We just didn’t execute. We’ve had trouble with lefties all year. He just kept throwing strikes and did well mixing his curveballs and changeups. We had runners on base almost every inning, but we just didn’t capitalize,” Lagios said. Game Recap Northgate scored once in the top of the first, third, and fifth, while tacking on two in the top of the seventh. The Broncos capitalized on mistakes, scoring in the fifth by way of a balk and one more in the seventh due to an error. Piedmont gained a runner in the bottom of the first when Diego Delventhal drew a leadoff walk, but PHS went down in order. Vo also drew a leadoff walk the following inning, but they the next three went out in order, once again. In the bottom of the fourth, Parker stepped to the plate as the leadoff man and turned on a pitch in a 2-2 count all the way to the right-center field wall. He legged his way all the way to third base, but Nate Luehs struck out two batters and forced a lineout to close the inning. Shafer Dando got a two-out single in the bottom of the sixth, but was left stranded. Michael Martin reached on an error with one out in the final inning of action, but Northgate retired the next two batters to end the game. Final stats: Parker went 1-for-3 with a triple. Dando went 1-for-3. Vo drew two walks. Delventhal drew a walk.

articles.text: MARKOS LAGIOS Football & Baseball At the annual Senior Awards ceremony, Piedmont High named Markos Lagios and Miya Fujimoto as the school’s 2025 Outstanding Senior Athletes recipients, noting their academic success, student leadership, and prowess in their sports. articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse closes out its 2024/25 season with The Sound of Music playing onstage now through June 29. The musical, based on the 1949 memoir The Story of the Trapp Family Singers, premiered years before the widely-popular 1965 American musical drama film. Berkeley Playhouse director Danny Cozart said the beloved, timeless musical is one of his all-time favorites that “continues to become more relevant day by day.” “The themes we are looking to explore in this production are the choices a person must make when the different structures of society [including] family, religion, and the state, are imposing conflicting demands on them.” Cozart said. “Our focus for this production is to drive home the real-world consequences of political action and the impact on a family trying to stay together in the face of looming tyranny.” Cast includes Marah Sotelo as Maria Rainer, Teressa Foss as Mother Abbess, Chloe Angst Danny Cozart directs Berkeley Playhouse’s production of The Sound of Music as Sister Berthe, Sage Alberto as Sister Margaretta, Akshaya Lakshmi as Sister Sophia, Robert Lopez as Captain Georg Von Trapp and Phillip Leyva as Franz. A cast of young musicians will perform the musical’s key songs. To purchase tickets, call the box office at (510) 845-8542 (extension 351) or visit www. berkeleyplayhouse.org. Showtimes vary. articles.text: Berkeley Symphony is hosting a concert this Sunday, June 1, at 4:00 p.m. in Zellerbach Hall. The concert will be conductor Joseph Young’s last concert as Music Director of Berkeley Symphony. The concert includes the Bay Area Premiere of Gity Razaz’ Methuselah (In Chains of Time), a piece that Berkeley Symphony co-commissioned. The piece promises to be a lush and poignant reflection on the endurance of life, inspired by an ancient Great Basin bristlecone pine tree growing high in the White Mountains of Inyo County in eastern California. Concert goers will enjoy Astor Piazzolla’s Concerto for Bandoneon, Aconcagua, featuring virtuoso Hanzhi Wang on the accordion. Drawing inspiration from the majestic peaks of the Andes, Piazzolla’s composition captures the fiery spirit of Argentine tango with its lush melodies and pulsating rhythms. To close out the season, Shostakovich’s monumental Symphony No. 5 serves as a stirring testament to the triumph of the human spirit over oppression and tyranny. From its brooding opening to its victorious finale, Shostakovich’s symphony resonates with themes of resilience, redemption, and the enduring promise of hope. Tickets may be purchased at https://www.berkeleysymphony. org/event/triumph/. Accordionist Hanzhi Wang will perform with Berkeley Symphony on Sunday, June 1.

articles.text: The Breshears String Trio will perform a concert at Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday, June 8, at 3:00 p.m. Imagine a family in which the first four children, all just a year or two apart, were eager to learn to play stringed instruments at an early age. All succeeded so well in the mastery of their instruments that as pre-teens and teenagers they performed frequently before paying audiences as soloists, duets, trios and quartets. The statistical unlikelihood of such a story is mind-boggling. And yet that is the story of the Breshears family. In the Piedmont concert they will perform works by Mozart, Handal/Halvorsen, Vivaldi/ Colton and von Dohnányi. The Breshears trio consists of violinist Valery Breshears (15), violist Colin Breshears (12) and cellist Starla Breshears (17). They reside with their family home in San Pablo. Valery and Starla are currently members of the San Francisco Symphony Youth Orchestra, which Colin will join in September. All are currently students at the San Francisco Conservatory of Music. The family in various combinations has been performing as soloists, duets, trios and quartets for 12 years. The sibling artists of the Breshears Trio also perform as soloists with orchestras all over California. These appearances have included California Youth Symphony, Kalamazoo Junior Symphony in Michigan, Palo Alto Philharmonic, Sonoma County Philharmonic, Symphony Parnassus, Nova Vista Symphony, Fremont Symphony Orchestra, Prometheus Symphony, Livermore-Amador Symphony, South Valley Orchestra, Diablo Symphony, and Diablo College Orchestra. As ensembles, they have performed throughout the world, including concerts in Argentina, Mexico, and Italy. In 2023, along with older brother and violinist Dustin Breshears, they performed as the Breshears Quartet at Piedmont Center for the Arts in a program entitled Beethoven, Borodin and Brazil. Tickets to the Breshears Trio concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on June 8 are available at brownpapertickets. com/e/6652231.

articles.text: San Francisco Opera presents John Caird’s acclaimed production of Giacomo Puccini’s most adored opera La Bohème onstage June 3 through 21. Puccini’s classic was the very first opera to be presented by the San Francisco Opera a century ago. The famous opera returns to San Francisco on Tuesday, June 3, taking audiences into the bohemian world of nineteenth century Paris to follow a group of ‘starving artists’ falling in and out of love and living for the moment. The libretto of La Bohème is based on Henri Murger’s 1851 novel, Scènes de la vie de bohème, a collection of vignettes portraying young bohemians living in Paris in the 1840’s. La Bohème’s debut at San Francisco Opera in 1923 catapulted it as a world-class opera company in the Bay Area, and was a favorite of General Director Gaetano Merola. Between 1943 and 1954, it was performed every season. This year’s cast includes Rene Pati and Evan LeRoy Johns as Rodofolo, Karen Ho and Nicole Car as Mimi, Lucas Meachem and Will Liverman as Marcello, and Andrea Carroll and Brittany Renee as Musetta. Visit https://www.sfopera. com/operas/la-boheme to learn more and to purchase tickets online. Call the box office for latest seating availability at (415) 864- 3330 for the June 7 and June 15 performances. Puccini’s masterpiece returns to the San Francisco Opera stage on June 3. articles.text: Photo courtesy of Randall Museum Randall Museum has something for kids of all ages. Randall Museum, a children’s science and art museum located in the heart of San Francisco, is offering discounted workshops for kids and teens throughout June in addition to free admission Tuesday through Saturday. The Randall Museum is operated by the San Francisco Recreation and Parks Department and the non-profit organization Randall Museum Friends and provides a unique experience for Bay Area kids of all ages, from pine needle basket-weaving to scrapyard robotics. Along with ongoing Saturday drop-in workshops for families, the museum is offering a new program entitled “Craft and Cinema” for craft enthusiasts aged 16 and up. Held on Saturday, June 21 from 2 pm to 4pm, this workshop invites craft enthusiasts and artists to bring a current craft project to work on while enjoying a screening of Chasing Coral in the Randall Museum’s theater. Crafters are encouraged to bring their crochet, knitting, embroidery or other projects to the movie screening and stay after to socialize and learn about Randall Museum’s many arts and crafts programs. In addition to a rotating list of art and science workshops held every Saturday morning, the museum also offers popular yearround exhibits open to the public throughout the week. The Museum’s live animal exhibit, Wild in California, offers an up-close look at California’s natural wildlife and is one of its most popular displays. Every Saturday morning, visitors can join in an open discussion about resident animals with wildlife ambassadors, and get an opportunity to meet Lyra the raccoon, who was born with several health problems including deformities of the spine and jaw, or a long-tailed weasel named Scarlet who was neglected and sustained injuries while in captivity. Lyra and Scarlet have been rehabilitated by staff and are now animal ambassadors for the museum. Visitors may also join a bird-watching exhibition any Saturday morning throughout the summer, guided by Dominik Mosur, who has the unique distinction of achieving San Francisco’s record for identifying the most bird species in a one year period within San Francisco’s 49-square-mile limits. articles.text: David Hen r y Hwang’s award-winning satirical play Yellow Face is playing on Shotgun Players’ Ashby Stage in Berkeley now through June 14. Yellow Face is a semi-autobiographical play featuring the author Hwang as the protagonist, DHH, mounting his 1993 play Face Value. DHH inadvertently casts a white actor in the role of an Asian character while taking a stance against racial misrepresentation in the media. The play’s themes include questions of race and of the interaction between media and politics. “This isn’t just a play about a single identity. It’s about how we perceive identity itself,” said Director Daniel Eslick. “My team and I are excited to create a space where audiences can reflect on their own perceptions. ‘Asian American’ is such a complex and layered term, but Hwang offers us a vessel to begin unpacking what that really means.” Inspired by real-life events, the comedy also explores themes of hypocrisy and the complexities of identity politics for second and first-generation Americans. “There are so many subplots to explore,” Eslick added. “Failed allyship versus expected allyship, Asian-American intersectionality, political relations with China, and many more come to the forefront in Hwang’s dense text. It all brings me to the question, ‘What is Allyship?’” Shotgun Players Artistic Director Patrick Dooley said the “whipsmart play … effortlessly juggles all these issues in a way that challenges us to consider our own responsibility and complicity.” “The fear and mistrust of China and its corresponding xenophobia that had somewhat cooled in the early 20th century is back on the front burner. And on a more metatheatrical level, the frustrations of artists from historically marginalized communities have taken center stage and demanded a reckoning with the American Theater,” Dooley added. Yellow Face premiered in 2007 and has since been hailed for its humor and social critique on race, politics and media. Hwang’s play won an Obie Award for Playwriting and a Pulitzer Prize nomination. Taipei, 1965) A large-scale exhibition featuring digital artwork by Yuan Goang-Ming, one of the foremost Taiwanese artists active in the international media art scene, is on view at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco now through July 7. Goang-Ming is considered a pioneer of video art in Taiwan and has worked with the digital art medium since 1984. He received the Hsiung-Shih Art Award for the Best New Artist for his video and sculptural work Out of Position (1987) when he was still in art school in 1988. He went on to receive a master’s degree in media art from the Academy of Design, Karlsruhe Germany in 1997 and has exhibited internationally across Asia, Europe, and America since. No advance reservation is needed. To join the tour, meet at the exhibition entrance on the ground floor at 11 a.m. Admission to Yuan Goang-Ming: Everyday War is required. By Allyson Aleksey Randall Museum, a children’s science and art museum located in the heart of San Francisco, is offering discounted workshops for kids and teens throughout June in addition to free admission Tuesday through Saturday. The Randall Museum is operated by the San Francisco Recreation and Parks Department and the non-profit organization Randall Museum Friends and provides a unique experience for Bay Area kids of all ages, from pine needle basket-weaving to scrapyard robotics. Along with ongoing Saturday drop-in workshops for families, the museum is offering a new program entitled “Craft and Cinema” for craft enthusiasts aged 16 and up. Held on Saturday, June 21 from 2 pm to 4pm, this workshop invites craft enthusiasts and artists to bring a current craft project to work on while enjoying a screening of Chasing Coral in the Randall Museum’s theater. Crafters are encouraged to bring their crochet, knitting, embroidery or other projects to the movie screening and stay after to socialize and learn about Randall Museum’s many arts and crafts programs. In addition to a rotating list of art and science workshops held every Saturday morning, the museum also offers popular yearround exhibits open to the public throughout the week. The Museum’s live animal exhibit, Wild in California, offers an up-close look at California’s natural wildlife and is one of its most popular displays. Every Saturday morning, visitors can join in an open discussion about resident animals with wildlife ambassadors, and get an opportunity to meet Lyra the raccoon, who was born with several health problems including deformities of the spine and jaw, or a long-tailed weasel named Scarlet who was neglected and sustained injuries while in captivity. Lyra and Scarlet have been rehabilitated by staff and are now animal ambassadors for the museum. Visitors may also join a bird-watching exhibition any Saturday morning throughout the summer, guided by Dominik Mosur, who has the unique distinction of achieving San Francisco’s record for identifying the most bird species in a one year period within San Francisco’s 49-square-mile limits. articles.text: A Simple Favor is a decidedly strange, neo-noir, character-driven film that engages and captivates throughout. The narrative is intimate and detached, with a twisty plot that is both intriguing and unrelenting. But what prove to be compelling are the performances of Blake Lively as Emily Nelson and Anna Kendrick portraying Stephanie Smothers. The setting is an almost archetypical Connecticut suburb. Emily and Stephanie are brought together by the nascent friendship of their first-grade sons, Miles (Joshua Santine) and Nicky (Ian Ho), who one day after school (their mothers arriving to pick them up), plead for a play date. Stephanie is immediately agreeable; Emily only reluctantly And so, two women are offered up that present an immediate and startling contrast to one another. Emily is vigorously confident, chic, works full-time for a New York fashion house and dresses the elegant part. Filled with attitude, she peppers her language with profanities and hard-edged commentary. Being a suburban mom to little Nicky is all but tangential to who and what Stephanie is a Betty Crocker surrogate – an apron would not seem incongruous. She’s perky, ever eager, having turned being a helicopter mom-classroom volunteer into an obsessive platform for her personal blog, appearing once Anna Kendrick and Blake Lively in A Simple Favor weekly with baking tips, crafts projects and personal homilies. The first afternoon play date takes place at Emily’s ultramodern house that is as stylish as she is, the interior decor mirroring her own starkly fashionable wardrobe. And it’s during the time the boys play upstairs that the two spend time on the wraparound sofa sipping (or in Emily’s case swallowing in one gulp) dry martinis with a twist, getting acquainted while sharing fragments of their lives. Stephanie learns that Emily is married and her husband, Sean, a once best-selling author with writer’s block, is presently in London visiting his ill mother. Emily learns that Stephanie is a widow, her husband having died in an accident. There are more secrets to come, but later. For Stephanie, Emily is a revelation, a direct, independent woman who refuses to let Stephanie apologize for anything. She almost instantly considers Emily her new BFF. But for Emily, ever enigmatic, friendship is an elusive emotion, a truth that Stephanie studiously ignores and so fills her blogs with Emily references. Days pass and it’s no surprise when Stephanie gets a call from Emily, asking her if she’ll take Nicky for the afternoon for a play date at her house. It’s a simple favor. Of course, and ever the good mom, Stephanie says yes, no problem. And it’s at this point that any comments regarding the plot should end. A Simple Favor, as it turns out, is a dark tale, of sorts, when Emily goes missing. With Sean in London, Stephanie finds herself unable to contact Emily and is unable to reach Sean. And so what was an afternoon play date turns into several days during which Stephanie grows increasingly worried. articles.text: Like its predecessor, Peter Rabbit, Peter Rabbit 2: The Runaway is a computer-animated hybrid, based on the much-loved books by Beatrix Potter. Kids love this rabbit, and The Runaway has an energetic, wack-a-mole, convoluted plot, set in great part in London and not the familiar Windemere farm. The story opens with the marriage of Beatrix (Rose Byrne) and Thomas (Domhall Gleeson), who, due to the efforts of Bea, are now living in relative harmony with the farm animals, most especially Peter (James Corden) and Thomas, whose trust of Peter is still a work in progress. Bea and Thomas have been working on a series of books that feature tales about the denizens of the McGregor farm. They receive a letter in the mail from a London publisher Nigel Basic-Jones (David Oyelowo). He wants to take Bea’s charming local stories commercial, a proposal that causes some concerns for the couple. But out of curiosity and to put to rest their questions about the methods to be used by Nigel, they take a meeting in London with the publisher, bringing with them not only Peter, but the whole crew: Flopsy (Margot Robbie), Mopsy (Elizabeth Debicki), Cotton Tail (Aimee Horne), and cousin Benjamin (Colin Moody). Peter, as it turns out, is not happy about the way he is portrayed in the stories, characterized as a bit of a rogue; Nigel refers to him as a “bad seed,” even villainous. So, in a pique, he leaves the group, only to hook up with some bad company, headed up by a rabbit named Barnabas (Lennie James). And so begins a series of adventures that take Peter first to Barnabas’ hideout where he learns that there’s a plan afoot to carry out a vegetable/dried fruit heist from the local farmers market. As it turns out, their carefully formed plans turn into a mess, wherein Peter and his clan get swept up by the Pet Pound, then freed, and head back to the farm where Peter seeks out the help of Thomas. They plan to return to London and defeat the underhanded works of Barnabas. Peter Rabbit 2 is exciting, slapdash, and even prankish, much to the delight of the kids who are happily watching events unfold, with tight corners gotten into and, of course, gotten out of. It’s all a lot of fun and the real-life animation is once again superb. Peter Rabbit 2: The Runaway. Directed by Will Glick. articles.text: It was a warm afternoon on Cinco de Mayo when the First Mondays Reading Group met for their monthly discussion at the Community Hall. The readers were there to talk about Cloudstreet by Australian writer Tim Winton. The novel was published in 1991 and has been called a classic. It has received several awards and was included in 2022 on the “Big Jubilee Read” list of 70 books by British Commonwealth authors. It has also been adapted into a stage play and a television miniseries. Cloudstreet tells the twenty-year long story of two poor, working-class Australian families, the Pickles and the Lambs. The Pickles family are struggling to rebuild their lives after being struck by disaster, when they inherit a big house called Cloudstreet in a suburb of Perth in Western Australia. After the father squanders the money that came with the inheritance, the family takes in the God-fearing Lambs as tenants for some income. The Lambs have suffered catastrophes of their own but are determined to survive. They open a grocery store on the ground floor of the house. Cloudstreet relates the families’ mostly shared post-war experiences from 1944 to 1964. They include drunkenness, adultery, death to resurrection, marriage, and birth. In the end, they are bonded together in this unique house. Cloudstreet was an excellent book group selection because some of the readers loved it, some liked it but had issues, and some readers disliked it so much they couldn’t finish it. For those with their thumbs up, it was “a great read” and “entrancing.” They enjoyed following the generations and their journeys. The book really is a journey. It follows the families’ challenges, their misfortunes, and their failings that result in generational trauma. The book’s occasional magical realism and supernatural events were left for reader interpretation. They also liked the cultural and character development. The possible motivations behind characters’ actions also generated an interesting discussion. This is an important book for Australians and readers with personal experiences in the country could especially relate to the story. Cloudstreet was not right for everyone. The readers were there to talk about Cloudstreet by Australian writer Tim Winton. The novel was published in 1991 and has been called a classic. It has received several awards and was included in 2022 on the “Big Jubilee Read” list of 70 books by British Commonwealth authors. It has also been adapted into a stage play and a television miniseries. Cloudstreet tells the twenty-year long story of two poor, working-class Australian families, the Pickles and the Lambs. The Pickles family are struggling to rebuild their lives after being struck by disaster, when they inherit a big house called Cloudstreet in a suburb of Perth in Western Australia. After the father squanders the money that came with the inheritance, the family takes in the God-fearing Lambs as tenants for some income. The Lambs have suffered catastrophes of their own but are determined to survive. They open a grocery store on the ground floor of the house. Cloudstreet relates the families’ mostly shared post-war experiences from 1944 to 1964. They include drunkenness, adultery, death to resurrection, marriage, and birth. In the end, they are bonded together in this unique house. The City is planning for 50 years and planting trees that will be able to thrive in a dryer, warmer, future Piedmont. After this overview, Nancy took the walkers to an upper park path and area where some of the reforestation had been done. Two new, flowering western dogwoods were in the center of an open area. Some of the group’s K-9 best friend owners noted the foxtail weeds in the area can get stuck in their pets’ eyes, ears, and noses and create health problems. Nancy understood the issue, but said the City has a policy of not using chemical sprays in its parks for control and she plans to ask the gardeners to cut back the grasses containing these weeds. Nancy took the group through the park to another newly replanted area near the popular tot lot. For one last park stop, Nancy showed the walkers a recently planted big leaf maple near the park’s restroom. Jean Hansen’s garden was the only Piedmont garden on the East Bay’s 2025 “Bringing Back the Natives Garden Tour” this year. Their tour is conducted on the first Saturday and Sunday of May each year. Jean told the walkers that her front garden is 98% native. The front garden was installed in 2008, and the back and side gardens were installed in stages, beginning in 2013. Jean was inspired by the initial “Bringing Back the Natives Garden Tour,” and she wanted to redesign her front yard which was inhabited by grass and camellias at the time, She replaced them with natives that include Coffee Berries, Manzanitas, Clevelandii Sages, Ribes, Epilobium (CA fuchsia), Irises, Heuchera, and more. They complement her rustic home and provide habitat for wildlife. Jean only has to water these native plants about once a month. They flourish on the slope that leads up to the house. Jean replaced a small lawn in the back garden with a native, mow-free bunchgrass lawn. The side and backyard have a variety of co-mingling edibles and natives. The gardens were designed collaboratively by Jean and several gardeners. She took the walkers up the side path to the backyard where the group also enjoyed its native beauty. The event began with an introduction by Mountain View Cemetery CEO Jeff Lindeman. Music then followed from the David Hardiman Trio as well as a short performance by the Piedmont Highlanders Drum and Pipe trio. Scout Troop 6 led the presentation of colors and pledge of allegiance. Then, Matt Camacho, bassist for the metal band Forbidden, played a bass guitar rendition of “The Star Spangled Banner.” Cemetery Trustee and the Reverand John Sutton, a Mountain View trustee, gave an invocation, followed by a proclamation and words by Cemetery Docent Dennis Evanosky. This year’s ceremony felt the watchful weight of history, marked by the 50th anniversary of the end of the Vietnam War era, and the 80th anniversary of the end of World War II. “These milestones offer a powerful lens to view the enduring meaning of a day like today,” said guest speaker Master Sergeant Tranquilino Herrera. “...
